Description: Valens is the eastern Augustus, raised to imperial power by his elder brother Valentinian in 364. Both are sons of Gratianus Funarius, but the burden of the eastern provinces now rests on Valens's decisions. He defeated Procopius's usurpation in 366, then fought the Goths across the Danube and reached an agreement with Athanaric. Success has not quieted his suspicion of ambitious commanders or unreliable reports. Persian pressure and the disputed position of Armenia draw his attention eastward, while troops and supplies are also needed elsewhere. He regards sound accounts and manageable taxation as foundations of stable government, yet demands close scrutiny of officials whose loyalty he doubts. His support for Homoian Christianity brings conflict with Nicene bishops and complicates relations within his own provinces. He wants imperial authority respected but cannot govern merely by declaring every opponent disloyal. A confident report may tempt him to act, while fear of concealed treachery makes delay equally attractive. He weighs a promise by its guarantors and a campaign by the men and revenue it will consume.

Motivations: Preserve Roman influence in Armenia without exhausting the eastern army or provincial resources.
Keep governors, commanders and churches cooperating under his imperial authority.
Values: Imperial legitimacy depends on effective government as well as titles and religious allegiance.
Military commitments must be weighed against revenue, provisions and dependable loyalty.
Fears: A disputed succession or another usurpation dividing the eastern army.
Pressure on the Persian frontier coinciding with unrest elsewhere.
